label: The customs union
depth: Outside it, and setting its own external tariff. But inside the Common Transit Convention alongside the EU27, and since the customs-security amendment of March 2021 inside the EU's Import Control System 2, which waives entry and exit summary declarations. Origin is governed by the pan-Euro-Mediterranean convention.
outstanding: Origin verification, tariff classification and customs valuation still fall on every consignment crossing to the EU. No published figure exists for what that costs Norway, and none should be invented.
contention: Not the primary friction. The customs border is administered rather than disputed.
source: European Commission (Taxation and Customs Union); EFTA

label: Competition and state aid
depth: As deep as it goes without membership. Substantively identical rules apply, enforced through the EEA's two-pillar system by the EFTA Surveillance Authority and the EFTA Court rather than by the Commission and the Court of Justice. Transposition deficit 0.7% against an EU average of 1.1%.
outstanding: The revised state aid rules, which would give the Surveillance Authority direct power to obtain confidential business information and to fine Norwegian undertakings for non-cooperation.
contention: Not which rules apply, but who enforces them and by what parliamentary majority Norway may agree to it. Opponents argue direct fining powers engage Article 115 of the Constitution and its three-quarters majority. The precedent runs the other way: on 31 October 2023 the Supreme Court held in HR-2023-2030-P that a simple majority sufficed for the ACER transfer.
source: EFTA Surveillance Authority, Internal Market Scoreboard No. 57 (30 November 2025); Supreme Court of Norway HR-2023-2030-P

label: Monetary policy
depth: Not applicable, and not by choice — this competence is exclusive only for states whose currency is the euro. Norges Bank sets the policy rate for the krone; it was held at 4.25% on 18 June 2026. Nothing in the EEA Agreement carries a monetary obligation.
outstanding: Nothing. ERM II is an arrangement for EU member states outside the euro area, so it is structurally unavailable to a non-member rather than declined.
contention: None. This is the one exclusive competence that generates no friction with a non-member.
source: Norges Bank

label: Conservation of marine resources
depth: Entirely outside the common fisheries policy. Managed instead by annual bilateral consultations with the EU — the 2026 round concluded on 18–19 December 2025, with the EU receiving 9,196 tonnes of Arctic cod and transferring 47,905 tonnes of blue whiting — plus a trilateral with the EU and the UK for North Sea stocks, and a separate bilateral with Russia.
outstanding: The trilateral framework agreement still does not exist. The 2026 agreed record notes the lack of progress in concluding one and commits the parties to finish by the end of 2026.
contention: Svalbard. The cod strand was settled on 11–12 November 2024, fixing the EU's quota at 2.8274% of the total allowable catch, or 9,217 tonnes. The underlying disagreement over the 1920 Svalbard Treaty and the legality of Norway's fisheries protection zone is de-escalated, not resolved.
source: European Commission (Oceans and Fisheries); EU–Norway–UK agreed records 2026 (Scottish Government)

label: The common commercial policy
depth: Full autonomy, exercised jointly through EFTA and bilaterally. EFTA's own dashboard records 35 free trade agreements signed with 49 countries and territories outside the EU; its FAQ page gives 31 agreements covering 42 partners in force. Neither page is dated and the two do not reconcile exactly.
outstanding: Norway has no free trade agreement with China. What exists is a narrower agreement on the import and export of food including seafood, signed 21 April 2017.
contention: Autonomy is real but has not redirected trade. Norway sends 67.5% of its goods exports to the EU — a higher share than Germany, France or Italy — after three decades of running its own trade policy.
source: EFTA free trade dashboard and FAQ (retrieved 6 August 2026)

label: The customs union
depth: Outside it, setting its own external tariff, and inside the Common Transit Convention alongside the EU27. Origin is governed by the pan-Euro-Mediterranean convention.
outstanding: Origin verification, classification and valuation on every consignment. No published cost figure exists.
contention: Low. An island with no land border faces less of the friction a customs border creates than Norway or Switzerland do.
source: European Commission (Taxation and Customs Union); EFTA

label: Competition and state aid
depth: Substantively identical rules, enforced by the EFTA Surveillance Authority and the EFTA Court rather than the Commission and the Court of Justice. But the compliance record is the weakest in the EEA: a transposition deficit of 1.5% against an EU average of 1.1%, and 120 open infringement cases against an EU average of 25.
outstanding: The same revised state aid rules Norway is arguing about, and the infringement backlog itself.
contention: The 120 open cases are the striking number on this page. Iceland already carries a larger compliance deficit than any EU member state average, in a country now asking whether to go further in.
source: EFTA Surveillance Authority, Internal Market Scoreboard No. 57 (30 November 2025)

label: Monetary policy
depth: Not applicable — the competence is exclusive only for euro-area states. The Central Bank of Iceland sets the policy rate for the króna; the seven-day term deposit rate was raised to 7.75% on 20 May 2026, some 550 basis points above the ECB's deposit rate.
outstanding: Nothing under the EEA. On accession Iceland would be committed in principle to adopt the euro, with no opt-out and no timetable — and Sweden has held that position since 1995 without ever entering ERM II.
contention: Not currently contested with the EU. It becomes a live question only if accession does.
source: Central Bank of Iceland; European Central Bank

label: Conservation of marine resources
depth: Entirely outside, and with no bilateral fisheries agreement with the EU of the kind Norway has. This is the single exclusive competence that decides the Icelandic membership question.
outstanding: A comprehensive coastal-states agreement on mackerel, absent since the dispute began and still absent.
contention: The relationship has inverted. In March 2014 the EU, Norway and the Faroes agreed a mackerel share that excluded Iceland. On 15 December 2025 a four-party arrangement between the Faroes, Iceland, Norway and the UK set a 2026 total allowable catch of 299,010 tonnes with shares of 30.55% to the UK, 26.40% to Norway, 12.00% to the Faroes and 10.50% to Iceland — and the EU is not a party to it.
source: Coastal states agreed records 2026 (Scottish Government); European Commission

label: The common commercial policy
depth: Full autonomy through EFTA and bilaterally. Iceland signed its own free trade agreement with China on 15 April 2013, in force from 1 July 2014 — the first such agreement between China and a European country, three months ahead of Switzerland's, and the EU still has none.
outstanding: Nothing outstanding. This is the competence where a small non-member has most visibly used its freedom.
contention: On accession the China agreement would lapse into the EU's trade relationship with China, and the negotiating capacity behind it would move to Brussels. That is the most concrete single thing Iceland would give up.
source: EFTA; European Parliament briefing PE 130631

label: The customs union
depth: Outside it, setting its own external tariff, and inside the Common Transit Convention alongside the EU27. Customs security runs through the 1990 agreement on simplification of inspections and formalities, amended in 2009 and again in March 2021 to bring Switzerland into the EU's Import Control System 2.
outstanding: Origin verification, classification and valuation on every consignment — and Switzerland sits geographically in the middle of the EU, so the volume crossing that border is large. No published cost figure exists.
contention: Administered rather than disputed. The contested Swiss questions are institutional, not tariff.
source: European Commission (Taxation and Customs Union)

label: Competition and state aid
depth: Shallow and sectoral. EU competition and state aid rules reach Switzerland only in air transport, under Articles 8 to 13 of the 1999 Air Transport Agreement, where the European Commission enforces them directly. Everywhere else the Competition Commission applies Swiss law. A cooperation agreement in force since 1 December 2014 lets the two authorities exchange confidential information but harmonises no substantive law.
outstanding: The 2026 package would extend EU state aid disciplines to air and land transport.
contention: Whether to accept those disciplines at all — part of the wider argument about how much EU law Switzerland takes without a vote on it.
source: EU–Switzerland Air Transport Agreement (CELEX 22002A0430(02)); Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs

label: Monetary policy
depth: Not applicable — the competence is exclusive only for euro-area states. The Swiss National Bank held its policy rate at 0% on 18 June 2026 and states an increased willingness to intervene in the foreign exchange market to prevent rapid franc appreciation.
outstanding: Nothing. No Swiss agreement with the EU touches monetary policy.
contention: None. The franc's strength is an economic problem for Switzerland, not a legal dispute with the Union.
source: Swiss National Bank (18 June 2026)

label: Conservation of marine resources
depth: Not applicable. Switzerland is landlocked and no marine fisheries competence is engaged. It is worth stating rather than leaving blank: the exclusive competence that dominates the Norwegian and Icelandic arguments is simply absent here.
contention: None — and its absence is part of why the Swiss argument is about institutions rather than resources.

label: The common commercial policy
depth: Full autonomy through EFTA and bilaterally, and the most active bilateral negotiator of the three. Switzerland's free trade agreement with China entered into force on 1 July 2014, the same day as Iceland's.
contention: Not contested. Trade policy is the area where the Swiss arrangement most clearly outperforms membership on its own terms.
source: EFTA; Swiss State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO)

label: Who enforces the rules — and by what majority Norway may agree to it
contention: The argument is not about which rules apply. Norway has taken the internal-market rulebook for thirty years. It is about enforcement powers moving to the EFTA Surveillance Authority, and whether that engages Article 115 of the Constitution and its three-quarters majority rather than a simple one. The Supreme Court answered that question for energy on 31 October 2023 and the challenge failed; the state aid rules put it again. Behind it sits the exposure: roughly 1.3 million tonnes of seafood a year go to the EU.
source: Supreme Court of Norway HR-2023-2030-P; EFTA Surveillance Authority

label: Fisheries — the one competence never tested
contention: The referendum of 29 August 2026 asks only whether to resume negotiations, and beneath it sits the exclusive competence Iceland has never tabled a position on. Chapter 13 was never opened between 2009 and 2013 because the Commission never issued the screening report. Iceland's own Foreign Ministry has put it plainly: the European Union alone holds the competence to conserve resources through its common fisheries policy.
source: Althingi þskj. 1245; Icelandic Ministry for Foreign Affairs summary of the negotiations

label: The threshold for approval — not the content of the deal
contention: The Federal Council wants an optional referendum. Parliamentary committees want a mandatory treaty referendum requiring a double majority of people and cantons, which would give small rural cantons disproportionate weight. On 11 June 2026 the Council of States declined to decide, 24–20, and sent it back to committee; a final parliamentary decision is not expected before 2027. Choosing the threshold very substantially chooses the outcome — and underneath it sits the same question that collapsed the talks in May 2021: dynamic alignment, and the role of the Court of Justice in settling disputes.
source: Swiss Federal Council; SWI swissinfo.ch (11 June 2026)
